sb_prompt: WHAT SHORT AND LONG-TERM STEPS DO YOU AND THE OTHER CALLER THINK SHOULD BE TAKEN TO IMPROVE THE US BUDGET?
turns: Yeah, so I'm just a librarian, not an economist, but honestly I'm pretty skeptical about this whole "fixing" thing right now. I've got this personal story about how my library budget got cut last year just to save a few bucks on something else. But then, what about you? You're younger, I'm guessing you've seen things from the ground up—how do you see the carpentry side of spending money?

Yeah, carpentry's different, I guess. Like, every time I finish a job and the customer's happy, I can spend that extra $500 on better tools or maybe save for a roof repair, but if the city cuts my permit fees or stops paying for street signs... well, you can't build a house without the wood or the nails, right?
Right, and I feel like we're just picking at the paint on the wall while the whole house is burning down. What do you think should be done first?
I mean, you gotta fix the foundation first, but honestly, we need to keep the lights on for a little bit longer so the workers don't starve while we're doing it.
That's a fair point, but honestly, I don't think we can even lay the foundation right now because the government keeps calling the blueprints 'too expensive' before we've even started digging.
Yeah, that's the thing though—we can't dig if the blueprints keep changing, but we can at least stockpile some lumber before the price goes up.

That's a real pickle, though. I know a lot of folks out there are just waiting for the next stimulus check to buy a new bookshelf, but honestly, if we keep throwing money at the problem without fixing the foundation, we'll just be buying lumber that's rotting in the rain. What do you think, B?

Look, I get the rot thing, but my big brother lost his job last month because the building codes changed overnight and he couldn't afford to retrain, so maybe we need a buffer zone before we tear the roof off his house.
Yeah, that's the scary part, isn't it? When the rules change on you so fast you don't even have time to pick up the phone and call your union rep.
Yeah, that's the scary part too, because once those codes change, it feels like the whole ladder you're standing on just disappears right out from under you.
Yeah, it's just that kind of feeling, like the whole ladder is vibrating so hard you can't even grab a rung before it falls away.
Yeah, exactly, it's like trying to balance on that ladder while someone else is shaking the building underneath you.

Yeah, that's the worst part, isn't it? You think you've got it figured out, you finally step up on that rung, and the whole thing just starts shaking so bad you forget how to breathe before you even fall. I mean, I get why we need some nails in the ground while we wait for the plans to settle, but throwing more money at the shaking floor just makes it wobble worse, right?
Yeah, that's the thing though, you can't build a solid house on a floor that's shaking so bad the nails are just popping out every time you hammer one in.
Yeah, exactly. So maybe the only smart move right now is just to hoard the nails and pray the floor stops shaking long enough to drive a few in before they rust.
Yeah, but if you just hoard the nails and the floor keeps shaking, you might end up with a pile of rusted scrap and no house at all.
Yeah, point taken, I guess... but honestly, if we just sit there hoarding nails while the floor vibrates us to death, what are we supposed to do?
Well, if we can't just do nothing, maybe we try to rebuild the floor piece by piece while slowly raising it up so we don't lose our footing, even if it means the house looks weird for a while?
That might work if we could figure out how to raise it without the whole thing just collapsing in on us first.
Yeah, but piece by piece is slow, and if the shaking gets worse before we finish raising it, we might lose half the floor before we even get the first plank set.
That sounds like a crazy gamble, though... if we start raising it now, won't the vibration tear everything apart before we finish the first plank?
Yeah, but maybe we start with the shortest planks in the middle where the shaking hits least, just enough to get us off the ground before we tackle the edges?

That's actually a good idea, middle first, but I'm scared we'll just build a new floor on top of the old one while the whole thing keeps sinking, and then we'll be stuck with a house two feet off the ground with no foundation at all.
Yeah, but maybe we just jack it up a few inches at a time, secure the middle, and then slowly edge out to the sides before the sinkhole eats the whole thing.
Yeah, that's the scary part, if we start hoarding the nails but the floor just keeps sinking faster than we can jack it up, we're gonna end up with a roof floating nowhere near the ground.
Yeah, but if we jack it up a little bit every week, maybe it'll just stay put long enough to get the nails in before the sinkhole swallows the whole thing.
Yeah, but if we jack it up every week and the sinkhole just keeps eating faster than we can hammer, we're gonna end up with a house floating in mid-air with nothing to hold it down.
Yeah, but maybe we just jacking it up a little bit every week, even if it looks crooked, so we can at least get the first few nails hammered in before the sinkhole swallows the whole thing?
That's a risky gamble, man, 'cause if it looks crooked enough to scare folks away, who's gonna pay for the roof?
Yeah, just make it look straight enough so people don't run screaming before we finish the job.
Yeah, but if we jack it up crooked just to keep it from floating away, maybe that's the only way to prove we're actually doing something before the whole thing collapses.
Yeah, I guess if it keeps people from running off the roof, then the crookedness doesn't matter as long as we can actually get the house standing before the ground eats us alive.
Yeah, but if we're gonna leave it crooked just to keep the roof from falling, I guess that's better than nothing, right?
Yeah, as long as it keeps the roof from falling, crooked or not, we're still standing, which is better than floating in mid-air.
Yeah, as long as it keeps people from running off the roof, crooked or not, we're still standing, which is better than floating in mid-air.
Yeah, I guess if it keeps folks from panicking, maybe a crooked house is better than no house at all.

Yeah, that's the thing though, if we just patch the roof to keep it dry but never fix the sinking floor, we're gonna end up with a house that leaks every time it rains and then we'll have to tear the whole thing down anyway.
Yeah, but maybe we just patch the roof real quick so nobody notices the floor's still sinking, then fix the foundation in secret while we're at it?
Yeah, but if we patch the roof in secret while the floor keeps eating us alive, we're just delaying the inevitable collapse until it happens right under our feet.
Yeah, but maybe we just patch the roof real quick so nobody notices the floor's still sinking, then fix the foundation in secret while we're at it?
